editions.description: Kristian Garza's technology radar edition showcasing the current state of technologies and practices.

blips.name: FastAPI
blips.description: Asynchronous Python framework that has reshaped not just how I work but how I think about API development itself. Perhaps the best framework at the moment for production APIs that need elegant concurrent request handling.

blips.name: Langchain
blips.description: Framework for accessing LLMs that many dismiss as unnecessary abstraction, yet proves useful—critically so—when products require flexibility to move between models. The abstraction, criticized though it may be, proves light enough to justify its existence.

blips.name: LlamaIndex
blips.description: RAG application framework demonstrating decent utility—not exceptional, but reliable—for both small experimental projects and medium-sized production services. Occupies that productive middle ground between proof-of-concept and enterprise-scale.

blips.name: Claude Code
blips.description: Marketed as a coding agent but actually a general-purpose agent whose features proliferate beyond easy summarization. The skills feature and context engineering approach are fantastic—so much so that everyone seems to be copying it now.

blips.name: Context7
blips.description: Embodies those rare concepts that benefit everyone if everyone participates. Places documentation in LLM-accessible formats via MCPs, creating a virtuous cycle of accessibility. An essential tool that improves the entire ecosystem.

blips.name: UX Pilot
blips.description: Used alongside designers to rapidly mock up interfaces with surprisingly smooth translation into Figma and development. My relationship with the tool remains more hopeful than established, more anticipatory than definitive.

blips.name: Figma and Playwright MCPs for Frontend Development
blips.description: A paradigm shift in the design-to-development pipeline. You forget immediately about traditional difficulties of translating Figma designs into functional code. Enables developers to move deeper into design while designers engage more directly with development realities.

blips.name: AGENTS.md
blips.description: Specification for normalized instructions for coding and databases—a vital, perhaps overdue effort to standardize what was becoming chaotic. Actively transforming repositories to this format, discovering clarity I hadn't realized was missing.

blips.name: Model Context Protocol (MCP)
blips.description: Method for accessing data rather than relying directly on APIs. I find myself genuinely torn—witnessing useful proliferation of tooling while encountering disadvantages needing resolution. Still, remains one of the primary solutions for making tools accessible to agents.

blips.name: GitHub Actions for Event-Driven Architecture
blips.description: GitHub Actions is not new—I have been using it for years in the traditional sense, for CI/CD workflows, the sort of automation that everyone expects—but nowadays I find myself using it mostly, almost exclusively even, to integrate services and orchestrate event-driven architectures, which has been, I must say without exaggeration, incredible. It has helped me create many services that I was previously considering less seriously, or perhaps not considering at all, services that now feel not just possible but inevitable.

blips.name: Eleventy (11ty)
blips.description: A framework for static websites, though mentioning only this framework seems reductive when what I'm really gesturing toward is that static site generators in general are proving remarkably useful now that we can spin up new apps so quickly, almost thoughtlessly. I have been using 11ty across five small websites and apps that take advantage of JSON as database and local storage together with the really quick—genuinely quick, not just marketing-quick—performance of an 11ty application.

blips.name: Bun
blips.description: Recently acquired by Anthropic—and this acquisition feels significant in ways I'm still processing—Bun is one of those executors that has been moving toward something incredibly fast, almost impossibly fast. It has definitely been something I've been using to replace many of my old projects, a migration that feels less like choice and more like necessity, the kind of technical evolution that makes previous approaches feel suddenly, inexplicably obsolete.

blips.name: Dia
blips.description: A browser I have been trying—genuinely trying, with real effort—to use, but I haven't been successful, cannot escape how good Arc Browser is in comparison, how Arc has shaped my expectations of what browsing should feel like. Still, once they migrate all functionality from Arc to Dia (and surely they will, eventually, perhaps inevitably), I probably will switch, but not at the moment, not yet, not while Arc remains what it is.

blips.name: ChatGPT Atlas
blips.description: The path I was hoping every browser would follow—exactly what I was thinking in terms of browsing, the sort of thing I have been discussing, sometimes arguing, occasionally banging my head against walls with colleagues about for months now. The problem, the persistent problem, is that it's still incredibly slow, and I think there's space—real, substantial space—for someone else to come in and do this properly. Not a replacement for my browser experience but definitely valuable for specific workflows.

blips.name: Claude for Chrome
blips.description: Without doubt—and I use this phrase deliberately because I have no doubts whatsoever—probably the best experience of an agentic browser that exists right now. Incredibly fast, doing everything you expect it to do and then some. My use has been limited so far, I haven't yet integrated MCPs or connected it with Claude Code, but I can see it integrating with many of the other things I've been doing, becoming part of an incredibly powerful workflow. I'm envious, genuinely envious, of how this came out and we didn't produce something like this before.

blips.name: GitHub Copilot
blips.description: Another coding agent similar to Claude Code—I have been using it for months, and it's been good overall, though 'good overall' is perhaps damning with faint praise. More specifically focused on development than Claude Code, which may be limitation or feature depending on your needs. I complain, perhaps too much, about the default prompts—I don't like the planning prompt at all and have to define my own. It has been falling behind in features: skills isn't there, agents isn't there, capabilities still coming. I'm definitely switching from Copilot to Claude Code, a migration that feels less like abandonment and more like natural progression.

editions.description: April 2026 edition covering LLM evaluation tooling, autonomous research loops, lightweight semantic search, and infrastructure deployment.

blips.name: Autoresearch
blips.description: Karpathy's autoresearch represents something I have been thinking about for a while but hadn't seen made so concrete—an AI agent given a real training loop and told to just run experiments, keep what works, discard what doesn't, and report back in the morning. The technique itself is the important thing here, not just the specific repo: you write the program instructions in a Markdown file, you set the metric, and the agent does the iteration. I have been using this approach in conjunction with promptfoo for LLM evaluation work, and together they constitute what feels less like a tooling choice and more like a methodological shift—one I'm not going back from. But autoresearch points further than evals, further than research automation; it points toward a mode of work where the human defines the objective and the constraint, and the agent runs the loop. That era, to borrow Karpathy's own framing, has begun.

blips.name: promptfoo
blips.description: I have been reaching for promptfoo whenever I need to test prompts, models, or RAG pipelines—and I find myself reaching for it often, more often than I expected. It runs locally, configures in YAML, and gets out of the way; the friction is low enough that evaluation becomes something you actually do rather than something you intend to do. Used alongside autoresearch it closes a loop: autoresearch runs the experiments autonomously, promptfoo provides the rigorous eval harness to measure whether any of it actually improved. The fact that it's now part of OpenAI feels significant, though I'm still processing what that means for its trajectory.

blips.name: SQLite with Embeddings
blips.description: For a long time I was reaching for dedicated vector databases whenever a project needed semantic search—Pinecone, Weaviate, the whole ecosystem—and then I started using SQLite with the sqlite-vec extension and something clarified. For small and medium projects, the vector database is almost always overkill; what you need is fast, local, zero-dependency semantic search, and SQLite with embeddings gives you that without the operational overhead of a separate service. I have been adopting this pattern across a handful of projects now and the simplicity of it keeps surprising me—not in a limiting way, but in the way that a good constraint surprises you by making the solution more elegant than you expected.

blips.name: SST
blips.description: I have been using SST to deploy infrastructure—it handles the Lambda function setup and the AWS wiring with less ceremony than doing it by hand—but my experience is genuinely incomplete, and I want to be honest about that. The Lambda-first orientation suits some of what I'm doing, but there's a class of architecture questions where I haven't yet had enough time with SST to know whether it would bend the right way or push back. My relationship with it is more exploratory than established; I'm inclined toward it, perhaps, but not yet prepared to recommend it with the confidence I'd want to have.

blips.name: Claude Agent SDK
blips.description: What the Claude Agent SDK makes possible—and this is the thing I keep coming back to—is that you can now build agents with the same tool execution loop, context management, and subagent architecture that powers Claude Code itself, programmable in Python or TypeScript, without having to implement any of the hard parts yourself. I have been using it to build agents that would previously have required significant scaffolding: you pass a prompt, specify which tools are allowed, and the agent loop runs autonomously—reading files, executing commands, searching codebases, spawning subagents for focused subtasks, and resuming sessions with full context. The fact that it recently got renamed from the Claude Code SDK to the Claude Agent SDK feels like honest clarification rather than rebranding; it was never just about code, and the new name says so.

blips.name: Claude Code Plugins
blips.description: I have been building and using Claude Code plugins for so many cases now that the technique has become something I reach for almost reflexively—a way of packaging skills, slash commands, MCP server configurations, and specialized agents into installable, composable units that can be shared and reused across projects. My own marketplace has grown to cover scholarly research workflows, senior software development patterns, and product management tooling, among others, and what surprises me each time is how much leverage a well-composed plugin provides—not just for my own workflows but for anyone who installs it. The technique itself is the insight: rather than configuring Claude Code from scratch in each project, you define the capability once, distribute it, and let it accumulate over time.

editions.description: November 2026 edition covering agent harness practices (context engineering, subagents, agent-maintained knowledge bases, model routing) and the tools around them.

blips.name: Progressive context disclosure
blips.description: My root CLAUDE.md is a short router: a table of where things live and a handful of rules, with each project holding its own detail. Skills and MCP tools load when they are needed instead of at session start. The habit that matters is resisting the urge to add one more rule to the always-loaded file. Thoughtworks moved this to Adopt in the same Radar, and my experience matches.

blips.name: Subagents for context management
blips.description: I delegate searches, test runs and log summaries to subagents so the main session only sees a short result. A routing table in my global instructions picks the model per task: haiku for read-only search, sonnet for specs and spikes, and the main session for design decisions. Parallelism was never the reason. Keeping tool output and retries out of the main context is.

blips.name: Agent-maintained knowledge bases
blips.description: My Obsidian vault is a PARA-structured knowledge base that agents read and maintain, with qmd (BM25, vectors, reranking, all local) as the search layer. Daily notes feed a task ledger, and weekly and monthly reviews are generated from them. The risk Thoughtworks names is drift, and I see it: some project notes go stale and need a periodic sweep to stay honest.

blips.name: Feedback flywheel
blips.description: When an agent gets something wrong, the correction goes into CLAUDE.md, a skill or a memory file so the next session does not repeat it. My verify-assumptions rule, the no-attribution rule and the shortwing stdin note all came from specific failures. It works for a single developer. Sharing it across a team is the part I have not tried.

blips.name: Coding harness for general-purpose agents
blips.description: I run non-coding work on Claude Code: task triage, daily briefings, calendar blocking, job-search tracking and flat hunting. Skills, hooks, subagents and MCP connectors already provide the loop, permissions and tooling I would otherwise build myself in an agent framework. For personal automation this beat assembling a framework.

blips.name: Grilling
blips.description: Before building anything non-trivial I have the agent interview me about the plan until the open questions are gone. It stops the agent guessing where my intent is vague, and it often shows me I had not decided something. I keep it as a skill that I invoke deliberately. On small tasks the interview costs more than it saves.

blips.name: Unattended agentic builds
blips.description: I hand a bounded piece of work to a background agent and review the result later, for example building a small library with tests while I do something else, or running a scheduled momentum sweep over stale tasks. It works when the task has a clear spec and a test suite to check against. The weak point is permissions: a job that needs one denied action stops at a push or PR step and waits for me.

blips.name: Stacked pull requests
blips.description: I use stacked PRs in some of my repos and find them useful: a large change becomes an ordered chain of small PRs, each targeting the branch below it, so every review stays small. Thoughtworks puts this in Hold. I disagree, at least for work where an agent produces big diffs that are hard to review in one piece. The cost is keeping the stack rebased when a lower PR changes, and I have only used it in some repos so far.

blips.name: Blanket frontier model usage
blips.description: Sending every task to the most capable model wastes money and adds latency. I route by task: bulk and mechanical work to the smallest tier, everyday work to the middle tier, and the top models only for the hardest design and judgment calls. I check current prices before routing by cost instead of trusting memory. Defaulting everything to the biggest model is the habit I am steering away from.

blips.name: mise
blips.description: mise manages my runtimes (node, python, go, bun, deno) and project tasks from one config file. Tasks cover small jobs like bundling a repo for an LLM with repomix, and just still handles some projects. Thoughtworks calls it a recommended default for development environments, and for my polyglot set of repos I agree.

blips.name: Herdr
blips.description: A terminal multiplexer built for running several coding agents side by side. A hook reports each Claude Code session's state back to it, so I can see which agent is working, blocked or done. I use it for real work and am still deciding whether it replaces tmux, which is still installed.

blips.name: OpenAI Codex
blips.description: I use Codex sometimes as a second CLI coding agent next to Claude Code. Thoughtworks has it in Adopt. It sits in Trial for me because Claude Code is still my main harness.

blips.name: OpenCode
blips.description: I used OpenCode for a while as a harness that works across models. I stopped when access to Claude through it was blocked, and I have not gone back. Thoughtworks keeps it in Adopt and recommends it for open-weight and local models, which is a different use from mine.

blips.name: RTK
blips.description: I set up RTK to compress command output before it reaches the agent. Thoughtworks warns that this kind of compression can break prompt caching and drop information the agent needs. I agree and have it on Hold.
